lead: Decide in advance: when this happens, I'll do that.
when: When your goal is clear but you keep forgetting to start, hesitate in the moment, or keep reacting in a way you don't want in the same situations.
body:
"I'll exercise more from now on." "I'll read when I have time." They sound sincere, but when evening comes, you often don't know at what moment to begin. Implementation intentions take a wish one step further: instead of only saying what you want to achieve, you agree ahead of time on exactly what you'll do in a specific situation.

An implementation intention is a way of planning that turns a goal into action by linking a specific situational cue to a corresponding behavior in advance, forming an "if this situation comes up, then I'll do this action" plan.

For example: "After dinner, once I put my dishes in the sink, I'll change my shoes and go out for a ten-minute walk." There's a cue you can recognize and an action that's clear enough. When the moment comes, you don't have to decide on the spot whether to do it today or what to do first. Getting started has a clearer way in.

The same approach can handle obstacles: "If it's still raining when it's time to go out, I'll do a suitable activity at home instead." The plan isn't meant to control every change, just to arrange ahead of time the step where you're most likely to get stuck.

The flow diagram starts from a recognizable cue and connects it to one concrete action. If there's a common obstacle, a simple backup path can branch off. What matters in the diagram is "when to start and what to start with," not turning your whole life into a complicated flowchart.
example:
You want to read every night, but you always forget about it while scrolling your phone. You could write the plan as: "At night, after I brush my teeth and put my phone on the charger in the living room, I'll read two pages by my bed." Leave the book somewhere within reach, and two pages makes it easy to know when you're done.

After a few days, you notice you often brush your teeth too late, so you change the cue to right after you've cleaned up from dinner. The plan has to fit your actual life. If you keep failing at the same point every day, check whether the conditions and the action suit you before blaming yourself for lacking willpower.
extra:
In meetings, when someone suddenly objects, you tend to jump in right away with explanations. You could decide in advance: "If I hear an objection, I'll first note down one specific concern the other person has, then check my understanding in one sentence."

This doesn't guarantee the conversation will go smoothly, and it won't make your emotions vanish instantly, but it gives you an alternative action you can practice. After the meeting, see whether you did it, then decide whether the action needs to be made simpler.
steps: Pick a small goal you genuinely want to pursue, and pinpoint the specific moment where you most often get stuck.
Write it as "If this cue happens, I'll do this action," making sure the cue is recognizable and the action doable.
Get the things you need ready and try it for a while, adjusting the cue or action based on what you record, and set up a simple backup plan if needed.
caution: It can't replace actually wanting the goal, or having the ability, time, and resources. A cue that's too vague, an action that's too big, or a goal that simply doesn't suit you can all make the plan fall through. Don't write dozens of rules at once, and don't decide it doesn't work because you missed it once; look at whether the setup is reasonable and what the real obstacles are.
exercise: Finish this sentence: "If ________, I'll ________." Shrink the second half down to a small action you can do today, and check that what you'll need when the cue hits is already prepared.
brief: A stick figure stands beside a clear doorway-threshold cue and naturally follows a navy arrow toward an open book and a desk lamp; where an obstacle appears, a simple backup path leads to a small doable step.
